His definition of the first, eloquence, is that it is the speaker's attainment, in conveying meanings, of a degree of which he has a distinction in fulfilling the special properties of constructions their due, and in presenting the types of simile, metaphor [majaz], and metonymy [kinayah] in their proper form. Then his division of fluency into that which pertains to meaning, which is the freedom of speech from obscurity [ta'qid], and that which pertains to wording, which is that it is Arabic in origin, proceeding according to the rules of the language, more frequent on the tongues of the eloquent, and more common in usage. Its form is:

Since you have come to know eloquence, and have found the semantic and verbal fluency, I will mention, as an example, a verse in which I will reveal to you the aspects of eloquence and both kinds of fluency that may be concealed from you. Then, if your taste assists you, you will perceive from it what those who were challenged by it perceived. It is His words, may His word be exalted: ﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water"﴾ to ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾.

(p-3442) The consideration of this verse is from four aspects: from the aspect of the science of figurative expression (ilm al-bayan), from the aspect of the science of meaning (ilm al-ma'ani) (these two being the foundations of eloquence), from the aspect of semantic fluency, and from the aspect of verbal fluency.

As for the consideration of it from the aspect of the science of figurative expression, which is the consideration of what it contains of metaphor [majaz], metaphor proper [isti'arah], metonymy, and what is connected to them, we say: when He, mighty is His authority, wished to express the meaning of: "We desired to return what gushed from the earth into its belly, and it returned; and to cut off the deluge of the sky, and it was cut off; and to diminish the water that descended from the water, and it diminished; and to decide the matter of Noah, which is the fulfilling of what We had promised of the drowning of his people, and it was decided; and to level the ship upon al-Judi, and it leveled; and We left the wrongdoers drowned," He built the speech on likening the desired to the one commanded who cannot, due to the perfection of His awe, be disobedient, and likening the bringing into existence of what is desired to the decisive command that takes effect in bringing about the intended thing, as a depiction of His great power, and that the heavens and the earth and these great bodies are subject to His will, in bringing into being and annihilating, and to His wish concerning them in change and alteration, as if they were discerning intelligent beings who have known Him with true knowledge, and have comprehended with certainty the obligation of submitting to His command and yielding to His judgment, and the necessity of exerting effort upon them in attaining its means. They conceive His increased power, so His awe is magnified in their souls, and His tent is pitched in the courtyards of their consciences. Thus, as His sign appears to them, the one signified is at once prior, and as His command reaches them, the commanded thing is at once completed, with no reception of His sign (p-3443) except by execution and submission, and no reception of His command except by yielding and compliance.

Then, upon this likening, He built the composition of the speech. He, may He be exalted and high, said: "(It was said)" in the manner of metonymy [majaz mursal], meaning by the will from which the saying of the speaker results. He made the indicator of the metonymy the address to the inanimate: "O earth" and "O sky." Then He said, as you see: "O earth" and "O sky," addressing them by way of metaphor proper [isti'arah] for the aforementioned likeness. Then He borrowed "swallowing" for the sinking of the water into the earth, which is the activation of the attraction upon the eaten thing, because of the resemblance between them, which is going to a hidden resting place. Then He borrowed "water" for "nourishment," by way of metonymic metaphor, likening it to nourishment, so that the earth may be strengthened by the water in producing crops and trees, as the eater is strengthened by food. He made the indicator of the metaphor the word "swallow" (ibla'i), because it is laid down for use in the sense of food, not water. Then He commanded, by way of metaphor for the aforementioned likeness, and addressed the command, as an entailment (tarshih) of the metaphor of the vocative. Then He said: "﴿Your water﴾" by attributing the water to the earth by way of metaphor, likening the connection of the water to the earth to the connection of ownership to the owner, and He chose the pronoun of address for the sake of entailment. Then He chose for the withholding of the rain "withholding" (iqla'), which is the agent's abandoning of the act, because of the resemblance between them in the non-existence of what had been. Then He commanded, by way of metaphor, and addressed the command, saying: "﴿Withhold!﴾", in the same manner as what preceded in "swallow." Then He said: "﴿And the water subsided, and the matter was decided, and the ark came to rest upon al-Judi, and it was said: Away﴾" He did not explicitly name who caused the water to subside, nor who decided the matter, nor who leveled the ship. He said "away" just as He did not explicitly name the sayer of "O earth and O sky" at the beginning of the verse, pursuing in each of these the path of metonymy, that these great matters are not accomplished except by one of power (p-3444) that cannot be comprehended, an irresistible Subduer. So there is no room for the thought to arise that it could be other than Him, may His greatness be exalted, who said "O earth and O sky," nor another who caused the water to subside in the way it subsided, nor another who decided that awesome matter, nor that the leveling of the ship and its settling is by the leveling and settling of someone else.

Then He concluded the speech with an allusion (ta'ridh), as an admonition to those who follow their path in denying the messengers, wronging only themselves. He concluded with an explicit statement, due to the place of wrath and the reason they deserved it, and that the calamity of the deluge and that awesome scene were only because of their wrongdoing.

As for the consideration of it from the aspect of the science of meaning, which is the consideration of the benefit of each word in it, and the reason for every advancing and delaying among its clauses, it is that "yā" (O) was chosen over its sister particles, because it is more frequent in usage, and because it indicates the distance of the one called, which the situation of revealing the magnificence requires, and displaying the matter of might and dominance. It indicates the distancing of the one called, which signals disregard for him. He did not say "yā ardi" (O earth) with a kasra, to supply disregard. He did not say "yā ayyatuhā al-ardu" (O you, the earth), for the sake of brevity while avoiding the artificial emphasis of "ayyatuhā," which is unsuitable to the situation. The word "al-ardu" (the earth) was chosen over the rest of its names, because it is lighter and more frequent. The word "al-sama'" (the sky) was chosen in the same manner as what preceded for "earth," with the intention of matching. The word "ibla'i" (swallow) was chosen over "ibtali'i," because it is shorter, and because the paronomasia with "aqli'i" (withhold) is more abundant. "Mā'aki" (your water) was said in the singular rather than the plural, because in the plural there is an appearance of abundance that is incompatible with (p-3445) the situation of revealing pride and dominance; and this is the reason for the singular of "al-ardu" and "al-sama'." He did not say "ibla'i" without the object, so that its omission would not entail what is not intended, namely the generalization of swallowing to the mountains, the hills, the seas, and all still waters, taking into account the situation in which the command arrives, which is a situation of greatness and pride. Then, when He had clarified the intended meaning, He abbreviated the speech together with "aqli'i" (withhold), to avoid superfluous filler that is unnecessary. This abbreviation is the reason He did not say: "It was said: O earth, swallow your water, and it swallowed; and O sky, withhold, and it withheld." "Ghīḍa" (subsided) was chosen over the emphatic "ghuyyida," because it is shorter. "Al-ma'" (the water) was said, instead of saying "the water of the deluge of the sky," and likewise "al-amr" (the matter), instead of saying "the matter of Noah," which is the fulfilling of what God had promised Noah of the destruction of his people, for the purpose of brevity and sufficiency, by the definite article in place of that. He did not say "it was leveled upon al-Judi," in the sense of "it settled," in the pattern of "qīla" (it was said), "ghīḍa" and "quḍiya" (it was decided) in the passive form, taking into account that the verb is in the active form with the ship in His words: ﴿while it sails with them in waves﴾ [Hud: 42], together with the purpose of brevity in wording. Then it was said: "﴿Away with the people﴾" instead of saying "let the people be distanced," seeking emphasis together with brevity, which is the descent of "bu'dan" (away) alone in the position of "li-ya'du'ū bu'dan" (let them be distanced, a distancing), along with another benefit: the use of "lam" with "bu'dan," which indicates the meaning that distance is their due right. Then He used the general term "wrong" to encompass every kind, so that their wronging of themselves enters into it, for the sake of increased emphasis on the atrocity of their evil choice in denying the messengers.

This is with regard to the consideration of the composition of the words.

As for the consideration of the arrangement of the clauses: He placed the vocative before the command, so it was said: "O earth, swallow! And O sky, withhold!" rather than saying: "Swallow, O earth! And withhold, O sky!", following what is required of one who is truly commanded, namely placing the calling before, so that the command that follows it may settle in the one called, with the intention of the meaning of entailment (tarshih). Then He placed the command of the earth before the command of the sky, beginning with it because the deluge began from it, and by its descent in that account it holds the position of the origin, and the origin is more deserving through precedence. Then He followed it with His words: "﴿And the water subsided﴾," because of its connection to the account of the water and its seizing of its hem. Do you not see that the original sentence was: "It was said: O earth, swallow your water, and it swallowed its water; and O sky, withhold from sending the water, and it withheld from sending it; and the water that descended from the sky subsided, and it subsided." Then He followed it with what is the intended aim of the account, which is His words: "﴿And the matter was decided﴾," meaning the promised destruction of the disbelievers was accomplished, and the rescue of Noah and those with him in the ship. Then He followed it with the account of the ship, which is His words: "﴿and the ark came to rest upon al-Judi﴾." Then the account was concluded with what it was concluded with. All of this is the consideration of the verse from the two sides of eloquence.

As for the consideration of it from the side of semantic fluency, it is, as you see, a delicate arrangement of meanings, and a conveyance of them that is condensed and clear, with no obscurity that trips up thought in seeking the intended meaning, nor any twisting that tangles the path to the seeker. Rather, when you test yourself upon hearing it, you will find that its words race ahead of its meanings, and its meanings race ahead of its words. There is no word in the composition and arrangement of the verse that reaches your ear without its meaning reaching your heart even sooner.

As for considering it from the standpoint of verbal eloquence (fasahah lafziyyah), its words, as we see, are Arabic, in common use, and follow the rules of the language. They are free from harshness (tanafur), far from ugliness, sweet in their sweetness, and smooth in their flow. Each of them is like water in its smoothness, like honey in its sweetness, and like the breeze in its gentleness. How wondrous is the matter of the Revelation! No scholar contemplates one of its verses without perceiving subtleties that cannot be contained by enumeration. Do not think the verse is limited to what I have mentioned, for what I have left out may well be more than what I have mentioned, because the aim was only the mere guidance toward how to gather the fruits of the two sciences of ma'ani (the science of meaning) and bayan (the science of rhetorical expression), and that no science in the field of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) after the science of usul (the principles of jurisprudence) is more useful to a person for grasping God the Exalted's intended meaning from His speech, more helpful in attempting the interpretation of its ambiguous passages, more beneficial in grasping the subtleties of its points and secrets, or more effective in unveiling the veil from the face of its inimitability (i'jaz). It is the science that gives the speech of the Lord of Might its full due of eloquence and preserves for it, in the places where interpretation is sought, its luster and its brilliance. How many a verse of the Qur'an you see has lost its rightful due and been stripped of its luster and brilliance when it has fallen into the hands of those who are not people of this science. They have taken hold of it in rejected ways and borne it toward unintended meanings, while they do not know, and do not know that they do not know. Thus those verses are in lamentation at their hands, and at their interpretations are in a long woe, while they think they are doing good work. This is the end of the words of al-Sakkaki.

Abu Hayyan also undertook, in his tafsir called (al-Nahr) [The River], to draw out its subtleties, and he cited twenty-one types of badi' (rhetorical embellishment). The Sayyid Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Amir composed a treatise on it called (al-Nahr al-Mawrud fi Tafsir Ayat Hud) [The Flowing River in the Exegesis of the Verse of Hud], in which he also set out those badi' types, namely: al-munasabah (appropriateness), al-mutabaqah (antithesis), al-majaz (metonymy/figurative usage), al-isti'arah (metaphor), al-ishara (allusion), al-tamthil (simile/analogy), al-irdaf (implication), al-ta'lil (causal justification), sihhat al-taqsim (soundness of division), al-ihtiras (precaution), al-idah (clarification), al-musawah (equivalence), husn al-nasaq (excellence of sequence), al-ijaz (concision), al-tashhim (completion of a phrase), al-tahdhib (refinement), husn al-bayan (excellence of exposition), al-tamkin (establishment), al-tajnis (paronomasia), al-muqabalah (contrast), al-dhamm (censure), and al-wasf (description).

And His saying, may He be exalted:

(p-3448) The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾

﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾ This informs us that Noah was moved by the compassion of fatherhood and the tenderness of kinship to seek his son's deliverance, because of the intensity of his attachment to him and his concern for his affair. Yet he observed, along with this, the etiquette of the divine presence (adab al-hadrah) and the propriety of the request. He said, ﴿and indeed Your promise is true﴾ and did not say, "Do not break Your promise to deliver my family." He said this only because he understood "family" to mean those related by apparent kinship and blood ties. Yet, because of his excessive grief over his son, he overlooked God's exception, ﴿except for one against whom the word has already preceded﴾ [Hud: 40], and he did not realize that his son was the one against whom the word had preceded. So he sought his Lord's compassion by entreaty, and he alluded, with his words ﴿and You are the most just of judges﴾, to the fact that the all-knowing, just, and wise does not break His promise.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 11, verse 46:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[46] ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family. Indeed, it is an unrighteous deed. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I advise you, lest you be among the ignorant."﴾

﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family."﴾ That is, the one whose salvation was promised, rather he is among those excluded because of their disbelief; or, he is not of them at all, because the basis of kinship (ahliyyah) is religious kinship, and there is no connection between the believer and the disbeliever.

Al-Qashani said: That is, your family in reality is the one between whom and you there is religious kinship, spiritual bond, and genuine rather than merely outward connection. As the Commander of the Faithful ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Verily, the friend of Muhammad (ﷺ) is whoever obeys Allah, even if his lineage is distant. And verily, the enemy of Muhammad is whoever disobeys Allah, even if his lineage is close."

﴿Indeed, it is an unrighteous deed.﴾ He clarified the negation of his being of his family by saying that he is unrighteous, as an alert that his family (p-3449) are the righteous, the people of his religion and law. And because of his persistence in corruption and error, it is as if he himself were an unrighteous deed. And it hints that the cause of salvation is nothing but righteousness, not his kinship to you in outward form. So whoever has no righteousness has no salvation. This is the secret of choosing "unrighteous" (ghayru salih) over "a corrupt deed" (ʿamalun fasid).

Yaʿqub and al-Kisa'i read (ʿamila) in the past tense, while the rest read it as a verbal noun (masdar), making it the very deed itself, for emphasis, as we have explained.

﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge.﴾ That is, do not seek from Me a request or a petition about which you do not know whether it is right or wrong, until you comprehend its reality. They said: The prohibition is only against asking about what one has no need for at all, either because it does not matter, or because the circumstances have made his state clear, as here; not against asking for guidance.

﴿Indeed, I advise you, lest you be among the ignorant.﴾ That is, I forbid you from being among them by your asking me about what you do not know. And at that divine admonition and Lordly reproach, peace be upon him, became alert, and sought refuge with His saying:

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[47] ﴿He said, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾

﴿He said, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge"﴾ i.e., from what issued from me. ﴿And unless You forgive me﴾ i.e., ﴿and have mercy on me﴾ i.e., by granting me understanding of what You love and are pleased with. ﴿I will be among the losers﴾ i.e., those who lost themselves by veiling themselves from Your knowledge and wisdom.

Note:

The apparent meaning of the revelation is that the son mentioned was his own son by blood. It is narrated from al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Baqir that he was the son of his wife, his stepson (rabib). Some have supported this with the reading of Ali: (And Nuh called out to his son) — and Allah knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, informed of what was said to Nuh, after the ship had come to rest upon al-Judi, with His words:

(p-3450) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[48] ﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon the nations among those with you. And there are nations whom We will provide for, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾

﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend"﴾ i.e., come down from the ship. ﴿With peace from Us﴾ i.e., with safety. ﴿And blessings upon you and upon the nations among those with you﴾ i.e., those in the ship who follow your religion and your way until the end of time. ﴿And there are nations﴾ i.e., and among them are nations ﴿whom We will provide for﴾ i.e., in this worldly life, because they are veiled by it. ﴿Then a painful punishment from Us will touch them﴾ i.e., in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

A subtle point:

The scholars have held various views regarding the Flood (al-Tufan). Most hold that it covered the entire earth. Others hold that it covered only the part of the earth inhabited by humans at that time, and others lean toward the view that it did not cover all of it and that not all humanity perished. Each group has proofs by which it supports its position.

Taqi al-Din al-Maqrizi said in (al-Khitat): All the followers of the revealed religions, the adherents of the prophets among the Muslims, Jews and Christians, have agreed that Noah is the second father of humanity, that the lineage of Adam (peace be upon him) was confined to him, and that God multiplied all the descendants of Adam from him. Therefore, there is no one among the children of Adam except that he is from the descendants of Noah. The Copts, the Magians, and the people of India and China disagreed with this, and they denied the Flood. Some claimed that the Flood occurred only in the region of Babylon and the western lands beyond it, and that the descendants of Kayumarth, who among them is the "first human," were in the eastern lands beyond Babylon, so the Flood did not reach them, nor India nor China. The truth is what the people of the revealed religions hold: when God saved Noah (peace be upon him) and those with him in the ship, he descended with them, and they were eighty men besides his children. They died after that without leaving descendants, and the lineage of Noah came to be through his three sons. This is supported by God's words about Noah: ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [al-Saffat: 77]. End of quote.

(p-3451) A similar account is in al-Kamil by Ibn al-Athir.

Ibn Khaldun said: They agreed that the Flood which occurred in the time of Noah and through his call swept away the civilization of the entire earth, with the destruction of what was inhabited, and that those who boarded the ship with him perished without leaving descendants. Thus all the people of the earth became his offspring, and he became a second father to creation. End of quote.

Some (in establishing the universality of the Flood, providing evidence for it) said: The waters of the Flood left remarkable traces in the visible layers of the earth. Marine sediments mixed with seashells are observed in various places, even on the peaks of mountains. In plains and deserts one sees animal and plant remains mixed with marine materials, some visible on the surface and some buried nearby. In caves, animal bones of differing natures and incompatible kinds have been discovered, along with remnants of manufactured tools and human traces, which proves that a flood carried them to that place, gathered them by force, and destroyed them. They became embedded between layers of clay and turned to stone, and remained as evidence of what had been, by the command of the Creator, exalted is He. End of quote.

The Mufti of Egypt, the Imam Shaykh Muhammad Abduh, was asked about verifying the universality of the Flood and the universality of Noah's mission, and he answered with the following:

As for the Noble Qur'an, there is no definitive text in it establishing the universality of the Flood or the universality of Noah's mission (peace be upon him). And what has come in the hadiths, even granting the soundness of their chains, are solitary reports (ahad), which do not necessitate certainty. What is required in establishing such realities is certainty, not conjecture, if belief in them is counted among the articles of religion. As for the historian and the one who seeks knowledge, he may attain from conjecture what his trust in the narrator, the historian, or the authority of opinion makes him prefer. What the historians and exegetes mention on this question does not go beyond the limit of trust in the report or lack of trust in it, and it is not taken as a definitive proof for a religious belief. As for the question of the universality of the Flood itself, it is a subject of dispute between the people of religions and the people of inquiry into the layers of the earth, and a subject of disagreement among the historians of nations. The People of the Book and the scholars of the Islamic community hold that the Flood was (p-3452) universal to the whole earth, and many people of inquiry agreed with them on this, arguing for their view by the existence of some shells and fish fossilized on the high mountains, because these things are formed only in the sea, so their appearance on mountaintops is evidence that water once rose up to them, and that would not happen unless it had covered the earth. However, most later people of inquiry claim that the Flood was not universal, and they have evidences for this whose explanation is lengthy. Nevertheless, it is not permissible for any Muslim person to deny the matter that the Flood was universal merely on the basis of stories about the people of China, or merely on the possibility of interpretation in the verses of the Noble Book. Rather, it is incumbent upon everyone who believes in the religion not to negate anything that the apparent meaning of the verses and the hadiths whose chains are sound indicates, and not to turn away from them to interpretation, except by a rational proof that establishes with certainty that the apparent meaning is not intended. Reaching that in such a question requires lengthy investigation, great effort, and profound knowledge of the layers of the earth and what they contain, and that depends on various sciences, transmitted and rational. Whoever is guided by his opinion without definitive knowledge is reckless, and his word is not heeded, nor is he permitted to spread his ignorance. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best.

Some have inclined to the view that the Flood was universal, because civilization was not established except among the people of Noah, so it was universal for them, even though in one respect it was particular to them, since there was no one else. He said:

Adam descended to the earth, and he was not a nation. When centuries pass over a nation, they give birth to nations. Rather, he was a single individual over whom years pass, indeed centuries, and the growth of his kin scarcely occurs except as a shadow gradually shrinks. From Adam to Noah there were eight fathers. If eight fathers produce descendants in multiples and thousands, until they tread the face of the earth with their feet and spread civilization in those days, then that is one of the greatest matters that history records as a wonder to the worlds! As for those mountains on which fish bones were found, if they were reached by the Flood from the specific place previously mentioned, then there is no proof. And if they were in other than that place, then if a human did not place them there, just as a human found them, it is possible that birds of prey and carnivores carried those bones to those mountains. By this and other things not hidden from understanding, you know that the Flood was particular and universal: particular to a place, universal to the rest of the place. And God knows best.

And His words, may He be exalted:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[49] ﴿That is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed, the final outcome is for the righteous.﴾

﴿That﴾ refers to the story of Noah, peace be upon him. ﴿Among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this﴾, i.e., the revelation to you and the informing you of it. Mentioning "your people" serves as a reminder that he did not learn it, since he did not mix with anyone other than them, and that they, despite their number, had not heard it, so how could one of them have?

﴿So be patient﴾, i.e., in conveying the message and in bearing the harm of your people, just as Noah was patient, and expect the outcome to be in your favor, and in favor of whoever denies you, similar to what was decreed for Noah and his people. So said al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf.

﴿Indeed, the final outcome﴾, i.e., in this world through victory and triumph, and in the Hereafter through everlasting bliss, ﴿is for the righteous﴾, i.e., those who guard themselves against polytheism (shirk) and sins.

The exposition of His words, may He be exalted:

[50] ﴿And to ʿĀd [We sent] their brother Hūd. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are but inventors [of falsehood]."﴾

﴿And to ʿĀd [We sent] their brother Hūd﴾: this is coordinated with His words "[Nūḥ]" [in the preceding verse]. That is: "And We sent [a messenger] to ʿĀd." The word "their brother" (akhāhum) means "one of them" (wāḥidan), as they say, "O brother of the Arabs" (yā akhā al-ʿArab). ﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah"﴾ — (p-3454) that is, Him alone — ﴿you have no deity other than Him. You are but inventors [of falsehood]﴾, that is, by taking idols as partners and making them intercessors.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[51] ﴿O my people, I do not ask of you any wage for it. My wage is only from the One who originated me. Will you not then reason?﴾

﴿O my people, I do not ask of you any wage for it. My wage is only from the One who originated me.﴾ Every messenger addressed his people with this, to remove suspicion and to make the advice pure, for advice does not benefit when it is mixed with greed. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ That is, will you not reflect, since you reject the advice of one who asks you for no wage, and nothing negates suspicion more than that? Or [it means] will you not ponder what is right from what is wrong?

"Concerning the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:"

[52] ﴿And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and will add strength to your strength. And do not turn away as criminals.﴾

﴿And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord﴾: that is, from standing with desire in shirk (polytheism). ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾: that is, from worshipping other than Him, by turning towards tawhid (monotheism). ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾: that is, abundant in outpouring, meaning rains. "Abundant" (midrar) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "the sky" (al-sama'). It was not made feminine although the word is feminine, either because what is meant by "the sky" is the cloud or the rain, so it is made masculine according to the sense; or because (mif'al) is an intensive form (lil-mubalaghah), which applies to both masculine and feminine, like "sabur"; or the ta' marbuta has been dropped from (mif'al) by way of the nisbah (relative form). This was stated by al-Samin. ﴿And will add strength to your strength﴾: that is, added to it or along with it, meaning intensity added to your intensity, through physical strength, or through wealth or sons. He only drew them to faith and encouraged them towards it by abundance of rain and increase of strength, because the people were owners of crops and gardens, eager to strengthen themselves by what was mentioned, due to the wealth they possessed, and to intimidate their enemies. They had been proverbial for strength, as they said: ﴿Who is stronger than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. ﴿And do not turn away﴾: that is, do not turn away from what I call you to. ﴿As criminals﴾: that is, persisting in your crimes and sins.

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[53] ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor are we going to believe you."﴾

﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof"﴾ i.e., any argument that indicates the soundness of your claim. This is due to the deficiency of their understanding and the blindness of their insight in perceiving the proof, because of the natural veils (al-ghishawat al-tabi'iyya) upon them. And when they do not perceive it, they necessarily deny it. ﴿And we will not abandon our gods﴾ i.e., their worship, ﴿on your word﴾. The phrase "on your word" (ʿan qawlika) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in (tarikī, "abandoning"), meaning: an abandoning that proceeds from your word. Or "ʿan" is causal (li-l-ta'lil), as in His saying: ﴿except for a promise﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], meaning "because of it," in which case it is connected to (tarikī). The first reading is more eloquent, since it indicates that it is an effective cause, which the particles "bi" and "li" would not convey. This is like their saying in al-A'raf: ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship?﴾ [al-A'raf: 70].

﴿Nor are we going to believe you﴾ i.e., we will not be people who accept your word as true. This is a declaration of despair to him regarding a response.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:**

[54] ﴿We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil.* He said: "I call God to witness, and you bear witness that I am innocent of what you associate*"﴾ [55] ﴿apart from Him. So scheme against me, all of you together, and give me no respite.﴾ [Hud: 54–55]

﴿We say nothing except that﴾, i.e., "has touched you," ﴿some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾, i.e., with madness, because of your reviling them, your turning away from them, and your enmity toward them, as a retaliation from them for your evil deed, with an evil recompense. Therefore you speak as you speak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Their previous answers show that they were coarse, hard-hearted, who did not care about slander, did not heed counsel, and whose obstinacy (shikima) was not softened toward right guidance. This last point indicates extreme ignorance and utter stupidity, in that they believed that stones could give victory and take revenge. ﴿He said: "I call God to witness"﴾, i.e., against me, ﴿and you bear witness that I am innocent of what you associate﴾ ﴿apart from Him﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the greatest signs is that a single man confronts, with these words, a nation thirsty to shed his blood, who shoot at him from one bow. This was because of his trust in his Lord, and that He would protect him from them, so that their claws would not sink into him. In a similar vein, Noah (peace be upon him) said to his people: ﴿Then decide your plan against me, and give me no respite﴾ [Yunus: 71]. He affirmed his innocence from their gods and their associating partners, and confirmed it by what is customary among people, who confirm matters by the testimony of God and the testimony of men. So a man says: "God is my witness that I will not do such and such," and says to his people: "Be witnesses that I will not do it." When he openly declared his innocence from what they worshipped, he commanded them to gather together and cooperate in carrying out a scheme against him, (peace be upon him), without delay, by his saying: ﴿So scheme against me, all of you together﴾ [Hud: 55], i.e., you and your gods, ﴿and give me no respite﴾ [Hud: 55], meaning: if what you hinted at is true, that your gods have an influence to harm, then be with them in it, undertake it, and I will hasten what you do without delay.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The fa' (then) here is for deriving the command from their claim about the power of their gods to do what they said, and for his innocence, both together. This is one of the greatest miracles, for he (peace and blessings be upon him) was a single man among a vast crowd and a great throng of the obstinate and harsh tyrants of 'Ad. He addressed them with what he addressed them with, belittled them and their gods, incited them to engage in the beginnings of opposition and harm, and urged them to take up the means of hostility and enmity. Yet they were unable to undertake anything of what they were charged with, and their incapacity became clearly evident. How could it be otherwise, when he had taken refuge in a mighty and exalted pillar, by saying:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:**

[54] ﴿We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil.* He said: "I call God to witness, and you bear witness that I am innocent of what you associate*"﴾ [55] ﴿apart from Him. So scheme against me, all of you together, and give me no respite.﴾ [Hud: 54–55]

﴿We say nothing except that﴾, i.e., "has touched you," ﴿some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾, i.e., with madness, because of your reviling them, your turning away from them, and your enmity toward them, as a retaliation from them for your evil deed, with an evil recompense. Therefore you speak as you speak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Their previous answers show that they were coarse, hard-hearted, who did not care about slander, did not heed counsel, and whose obstinacy (shikima) was not softened toward right guidance. This last point indicates extreme ignorance and utter stupidity, in that they believed that stones could give victory and take revenge. ﴿He said: "I call God to witness"﴾, i.e., against me, ﴿and you bear witness that I am innocent of what you associate﴾ ﴿apart from Him﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the greatest signs is that a single man confronts, with these words, a nation thirsty to shed his blood, who shoot at him from one bow. This was because of his trust in his Lord, and that He would protect him from them, so that their claws would not sink into him. In a similar vein, Noah (peace be upon him) said to his people: ﴿Then decide your plan against me, and give me no respite﴾ [Yunus: 71]. He affirmed his innocence from their gods and their associating partners, and confirmed it by what is customary among people, who confirm matters by the testimony of God and the testimony of men. So a man says: "God is my witness that I will not do such and such," and says to his people: "Be witnesses that I will not do it." When he openly declared his innocence from what they worshipped, he commanded them to gather together and cooperate in carrying out a scheme against him, (peace be upon him), without delay, by his saying: ﴿So scheme against me, all of you together﴾ [Hud: 55], i.e., you and your gods, ﴿and give me no respite﴾ [Hud: 55], meaning: if what you hinted at is true, that your gods have an influence to harm, then be with them in it, undertake it, and I will hasten what you do without delay.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The fa' (then) here is for deriving the command from their claim about the power of their gods to do what they said, and for his innocence, both together. This is one of the greatest miracles, for he (peace and blessings be upon him) was a single man among a vast crowd and a great throng of the obstinate and harsh tyrants of 'Ad. He addressed them with what he addressed them with, belittled them and their gods, incited them to engage in the beginnings of opposition and harm, and urged them to take up the means of hostility and enmity. Yet they were unable to undertake anything of what they were charged with, and their incapacity became clearly evident. How could it be otherwise, when he had taken refuge in a mighty and exalted pillar, by saying:

(p-3457) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[56] ﴿Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.﴾

﴿Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ meaning: so you cannot reach me with any harm, because of my reliance upon Allah. ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ meaning: He owns it, has power over it, and turns it however He wills.

Al-Qashani (al-Qashani) said: He made clear the obligation of relying upon Allah and that it is an impregnable fortress, first by [showing] that His lordship encompasses everyone, and whoever is a lord manages the affairs of what is lordly over him and protects it, so it has no need for the guardianship and protection of another. Then [He showed] that every living being is under His subjugation and authority, a captive in the hand of His disposal, His dominion and His power, unable to act, to have strength, or to have influence over others, having no movement of its own, like the dead; so there is no need to guard against it. -End-

The forelock (al-nasiyah): the place where hair grows at the front of the head, and it is also used for the hair growing there, by naming the thing after its place. It is said: "nasawtu al-rajul" (I seized the man by his forelock), meaning I took hold of his forelock.

In (al-'Inayah): The saying of people, "his forelock is in his hand," means he is submissive to him. Seizing by the forelock is an expression for power and dominance, either metaphorically or as a metonymy.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾, it is a justification for what reliance implies, namely their inability to harm him: that is, He is upon the way of truth and justice in His dominion, so He will not give you power over me, for the one who holds fast to Him is not lost before Him, and no wrongdoer escapes Him.

In (al-'Inayah) it says: This is an image and a metaphor, because He is aware of the affairs of His servants, rewarding and punishing them, and sufficient for whoever holds fast to Him, like one who stands upon the main road and guards it, and thereby repels harm from travelers.

(p-3458) This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. The restriction of the attribution of the Lord to Himself is either by way of sufficiency, since the intended meaning is clear, or to indicate that gentleness and aid are specific to Him alone, not to them.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[57] ﴿And if you turn away, then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will bring about in your place a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.﴾

﴿And if you turn away﴾ meaning: if you (persist in) turning away, with one of the two tā' elided. ﴿then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you﴾ meaning: the proof has been established against you. ﴿And my Lord will bring about in your place a people other than you﴾ is a resumption (istinaf) containing a threat against them, meaning: He will destroy them and bring other people who will succeed you in your homes and your wealth. ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾ meaning: by your turning away, because that is impossible for Him; rather, you harm yourselves. Or, by your departing and your destruction, nothing diminishes from His dominion. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things﴾ meaning: He is Watcher over it, Overseer, so your deeds are not hidden from Him, and He will recompense you according to them; or, He is Preserver, Governing, having dominion over all things, so nothing can harm Him.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[58] ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment.﴾

﴿When Our command came﴾ — that is, Our punishment, or Our command with the punishment, which was the barren wind (al-rih al-'aqim).

﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment﴾. It has been explained in other verses, among them His saying: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious, violent wind﴾ [al-Haqqah: 6], ﴿which He unleashed against them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you could see the people lying prostrate in it as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7].

(p-3459) If you ask: what is the meaning of the repetition of "saving"? The answer: there is no repetition in it, for the first is an announcement that their salvation was by the mercy and bounty of God, while the second is a statement of what they were saved from, namely a matter that is severe and great, not easy. So it is a reminder of favour to them and an incitement to them to believe. Or, the first is salvation from the punishment of this world, and the second from the punishment of the Hereafter, by way of allusion that just as the destroyed were punished in this world by the scorching wind, so they will be punished in the Hereafter with the harsh punishment. The first is preferred, because it fits the requirement of the context.

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[59] ﴿And those were 'Ad, who denied the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾

﴿And those were 'Ad, who denied the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers﴾: The demonstrative *tilka* (تِلْكَ, "that") is feminine, in view of the tribe (القبيلة). The form of the distant demonstrative (صيغة البعيد) is used either to belittle them or to place them in the position of the distant, because of their insignificance. If the demonstrative refers to their place of destruction (مصارعهم), then it indicates the distant that is perceptible (البعيد المحسوس). The verb *jahadu* (جَحَدُوا, "denied") takes the preposition *bi-* (بِ) because it is treated as "disbelieved" (حملاً له على الكفر), since that is what is meant. Alternatively, it takes that preposition by implying a meaning of its own (بتضمينه معناه), just as *kafara* (كَفَرَ, "disbelieved") is used in the manner of *jahada*. Thus it takes a direct object without a preposition in His words ﴿disbelieved in their Lord﴾ [Hud: 60]. It has been said that *kafara*, like *shakara* (شَكَرَ), takes an object both directly and with a preposition. The apparent sense of the words of al-Qamus (القاموس, "the Dictionary") is that *jahada* is likewise.

The meaning is: they disbelieved in God and rejected His signs, which are in themselves and on the horizons, indicating His oneness. The plural *al-rusul* (الرُّسُلِ, "the messengers") is used, although only Hud, upon him be blessings and peace, was sent to them. This is to express the abhorrence of their condition and to show the completeness of their disbelief and obstinacy, by clarifying that their disobedience to him, upon him be blessings and peace, is disobedience to all the messengers, both those before him and those after him, because their word is united upon monotheism: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqara: 285]. So says al-Inaya (العناية, "the Care"), and Abu al-Su'ud (أبو السعود, "Abu al-Su'ud"), (the tafsir).

(p-3460) ﴿And followed﴾, that is, obeyed in polytheism, ﴿the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾ who is not guided by any proof and does not accept it from anyone else. He means their leaders and their elders, and their callers to denying the messengers.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[60] ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with ʿAd, the people of Hud.﴾

﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection﴾ That is, it was made to follow them in both abodes, meaning it would be constant (lazimah) for them.

Abu al-Suʿud said: The expression of this by "following" (al-tabaʿiyyah) is for emphasis, as if it never parts from them, even if they go in every direction; rather, it revolves with them wherever they turn. It also occurs in the company of their following their leaders, meaning: since they followed them, they were followed by this as a fitting recompense.

﴿Unquestionably, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord﴾ by worshipping other than Him (and the transitive use of "disbelieved" [kafara] has already been mentioned): ﴿Unquestionably, away with ʿAd, the people of Hud﴾ He invoked upon them destruction or a curse, and in this there is an indication of the wrath and abhorrence directed at them, the gravity of which is not hidden. The repetition of the particle of alerting and the restatement of "ʿAd" serve to emphasize the magnitude of their condition and to urge reflection upon their account. "The people of Hud" is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ʿAd," its benefit being attribution to him, peace be upon him, through whose mission they deserved destruction; as if it were said: ʿAd, the people of Hud, who denied him. This also suits the verses in context, for before it is: ﴿And they followed the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾ [Hud: 59], and before that come "Hafiz" and "Ghalid," and other words of the pattern fa'il (faʿīl), which corresponds to fa'ul (faʿūl) in rhyme. And God knows best.

(p-٣٤٦١) The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil, explanation of the meaning) of His saying, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He produced you from the earth and settled you in it. So seek His forgiveness and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."﴾

﴿And to Thamud﴾ is conjoined to what was explained earlier from His saying: ﴿And to 'Ad﴾ [Hud: 50], i.e., and We sent [a messenger] to Thamud, which is a tribe of the Arabs. ﴿Their brother Salih, who said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He produced you from the earth,"﴾ i.e., He brought you into being from it alone, for He created Adam, and the material of the drops of semen from which He created his offspring, from dust. ﴿And settled you in it﴾ i.e., made you dwell in it, or made you its builders, meaning He made you able to build it, like His saying, exalted is He, in al-A'raf: ﴿And He settled you in the land, taking from its plains palaces and carving out the mountains as homes﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]. ﴿So seek His forgiveness﴾ i.e., from shirk (associating partners with Allah), ﴿then repent to Him﴾ by affirming His oneness (tawhid). ﴿Indeed, my Lord is near﴾ i.e., near in mercy to whoever seeks His forgiveness, ﴿responsive﴾ i.e., accepting his supplication.

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

[62] ﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾

﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this"﴾ That is, signs of goodness and indications of right guidance used to appear in you, so we hoped you would benefit us, that you would be consulted in affairs and sought for guidance in plans. But when you uttered this statement, our hope in you was cut off, and we knew that there was no good in you. Thus [says] al-Kashshaf.

(p-3462) ﴿Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?﴾ That is, of the idols. ﴿Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us﴾ That is, of monotheism (tawhid). ﴿Disquieting﴾ means causing unease (rayba), and rayba is the restlessness of the soul and the absence of tranquility.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[63] ﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will protect me from Allah if I disobey Him? You would only add to me loss.">﴾

﴿He said, "O my people, tell me"﴾ i.e., inform me. ﴿"If I am upon clear proof"﴾ i.e., an evident argument, and a manifest demonstration and insight ﴿"from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself"﴾ i.e., guidance and prophethood, ﴿"then who will protect me from Allah"﴾ i.e., who will save me from His punishment, ﴿"if I disobey Him"﴾ i.e., by complying with you in your desires. ﴿"Then you would add nothing to me"﴾ i.e., by your leading me to follow you, ﴿"but loss"﴾ i.e., you would only make me a loser by exposing me to the wrath of Allah. Or: "Then you would add nothing to me, by what you say, except to make you perceive [that you are] losers"—by attributing to you the loss.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[64] ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.﴾

﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah﴾: the idafah (attributive construction) is for honour and for informing that she is distinguished from what resembles her in creation and character. ﴿A sign for you﴾: i.e., a miracle indicating the truth of my prophethood. ﴿So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you﴾: from the intensity of Allah's anger against you, for your audacity towards His signs that are ascribed to Him.

Then He informed that they did not heed His words, nor obeyed, after seeing this sign, so He, glorified is He, said:

(p-3463) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[65] ﴿But they hamstrung her. So he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: i.e., they killed her. ﴿So he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾: i.e., not to be rejected.

Al-Qasimi said in (al-Iklil): It is cited as evidence for granting an opponent or the like a respite of three [days]. In it is evidence that (al-mithlatha, the number three) has a standing in the Shari'ah, and for this reason it was prescribed in (al-khiyar, the option period in sales) and the like.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[66] ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾

﴿When Our command came﴾ i.e., Our punishment, which was the Blast (al-Sayha), as will be explained. ﴿We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy﴾ i.e., because of a great mercy ﴿from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day﴾, which was their destruction by the Blast. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty﴾ i.e., the Capable of everything, and the Dominant over it.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[67] ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong, so they became lifeless in their homes, prostrate.﴾

﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾, i.e., from the direction of the sky, so they quaked at it with the quaking of destruction. ﴿So they became lifeless in their homes, prostrate﴾, i.e., motionless, dead, not moving. And there is no concealing what this indicates of the severity of the seizing and its swiftness.

**The discussion of His words, exalted is He:**

[68] ﴿As if they had never flourished therein. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾

﴿As if they had never flourished﴾: that is, as if they had never dwelt ﴿therein﴾, meaning in their dwellings. ﴿Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord﴾: that is, so He destroyed them. ﴿Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾: that is, destruction and curse, because of their distance from His path. We have already discussed the detailed account of their story in Surah al-A'raf, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary, so let it be consulted there.

Then Exalted is He pointed to the story of Lut and the destruction of his people, which is the fourth of the accounts in this surah, with His words, glorified is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[69] ﴿And Our messengers came to Abraham with glad tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and it was not long before he brought a roasted calf.﴾

﴿And Our messengers came﴾, that is, the angels whom We sent to destroy the people of Lot. ﴿to Abraham with glad tidings﴾, that is, with a son and a grandson. Then He explained that they put before the glad tidings something that conveys joy, so that the glad tidings would be joy upon joy, through His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Peace"﴾, that is, "We greet you with peace." ﴿He said, "Peace"﴾, that is, "Peace be upon you," or "Peace is upon you." He raised it (into the nominal form), answering with a greeting better than theirs, because the nominal form is more indicative of permanence than the accusative form.

Then He pointed to the goodness of their hospitality through His saying: ﴿it was not long before he brought a roasted calf﴾, that is, a grilled one, or a fat one whose fat drips, in accordance with His saying: ﴿a fattened calf﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 26].

There are three possible readings of (ma) (in ﴿fa-ma labitha an jaa﴾). The most apparent is that it is a negation particle. The subject of (labitha) is then either the pronoun referring to (Ibrahim), and ﴿an jaa﴾ is taken as governed by a preposition attached to it, meaning: he did not delay in, or with respect to, or from (an jaa), that is, in his coming; or it is ﴿an jaa﴾ itself, meaning: so he did not delay, and his coming with a calf was not late. The second reading is that (ma) is a verbal particle (masdariyya), which turns the following clause into a verbal noun. The third reading is that (ma) carries the meaning of (alladhi, "that which"), and in both cases it is the subject (mubtada'), while (an jaa) is its predicate (khabar), with an omitted first term of a genitive construction. That is: "so his lingering was (equal to) the time of his coming," or "what lingered for him was the amount of time of his coming."

(p-3465) On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[70] ﴿So when he saw that their hands did not reach toward it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot."﴾

﴿So when he saw that their hands did not reach toward it﴾ means: they did not extend their hands toward it. ﴿He regarded them with suspicion﴾ means: he found them strange (ankarahum). ﴿And felt a fear of them﴾ means: he sensed (ahassa) fear of them, supposing that they were humans who intended some harm to him. And a guest, when he intends to kill his host, does not eat the food; this was their custom. ﴿They said﴾ means: to him, when they recognized from him the fear, through his informing them of it, as in the verse ﴿He said, "Indeed, we are apprehensive of you"﴾ [al-Hijr: 52], ﴿They said, "Do not be apprehensive"﴾ [al-Hijr: 53], just as it is said here, ﴿Do not fear﴾, meaning: we do not eat because we are angels, and we have not come down with the punishment upon you. ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ meaning: to destroy them.

The discussion on the interpretation of His, exalted is He, saying:

[71] ﴿And his wife was standing, and she laughed, so We gave her the good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.﴾

﴿And his wife was standing, and she laughed﴾ meaning, out of joy at the departure of fear, or at the destruction of the people of wickedness. ﴿So We gave her the good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ meaning, he would be born to him. The two names may have been mentioned in the glad tidings itself, or she may have related them after they were born and were named so. As for directing the glad tidings to her here, even though the glad tidings came to Abraham in another verse, such as ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾ [al-Saffat: 101] and ﴿and they gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 28], it indicates her sharing with Abraham in that at the time of their arrival, and it points to the fact that mentioning one of them suffices for the other. The context is also more fitting for its mention and more eloquent. Or it is to arrive at narrating her story in this and the breaking of custom in it, as her wonder is hinted at in His saying, exalted is He:

(p-3466) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[72] ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman, and this, my husband, is an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾

﴿She said, "Woe to me!"﴾ That is, "O my wonder!" Its original usage is as a supplication invoking woe or the like, in the cry of lamentation at a severe calamity that overwhelms the soul; then it was used to express amazement. Its alif is a substitute for the ya' of the speaker, and for this reason Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in one narration inclined it (ya waylataya/ya waylati), and al-Hasan recited it as (ya waylati). It is also said that it is the alif of nudba (lamenting invocation), and it is pausally stopped upon with the haa' al-sakt (the silent haa').

﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman﴾ That is, a woman advanced in years — and the more eloquent usage is to omit the haa' with it (i.e., 'ajuz rather than 'ajuzah) — and it has been heard from some Arabs (ʿajūzah), related by Yunus. ﴿And this, my husband﴾ That is, my spouse Ibrahim, ﴿is an old man. Indeed, this﴾ — that is, bearing a child from two aged persons — ﴿is an astonishing thing﴾ That is, strange, something for which the usual course of things has not been established.

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:

[73] ﴿They said: "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, Glorious."﴾

﴿They said, "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah?"﴾ That is: Do you deem it far-fetched, concerning His affair and His power, that He should create a child from two aged people?

Al-Zamakhshari said: The angels only denied her wonder because she was in the house of signs, the place of descent of miracles and of matters that break customary habits. It was therefore incumbent upon her to be dignified and not to be delighted by what delights other women who grow up outside the house of prophethood, and to glorify and praise Allah in place of wonder. The angels, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, alluded to this in their words: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house.﴾ They meant that such things, and their like, are what the Lord of Might honours you with and singles you out to be favoured with, O people of the house of prophethood, so they are not a matter for wonder. The statement is a new sentence (mustaʼnaf), given as a reason (ta'līl) for the denial of wonder, as if it were said: "Beware of wonder," for the like of this mercy and blessing from Allah upon you is abundant. [End of quotation.]

The sentence is declarative (khabariyyah), and he permitted that it be supplicatory (du'a'iyyah). The phrase (ahla al-bayt) is in the accusative either as a vocative (nida') or as a specification (takhsis), because "people of the house" is a form of praise for them, since what is meant is the people of the house of the Friend of the Most Merciful (Khalil al-Rahman, i.e., Abraham).

﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy﴾ That is, He deserves praise for the great blessings He has bestowed. ﴿Glorious﴾ That is, Generous, of vast benevolence, so it is not far-fetched that He should give a child after old age. This is a wonderful concluding phrase (tadhyil) explaining that the requirement of her situation is that she should praise the One deserving of praise, who has done good to her in what He has done well, and glorify Him, since He has honoured her with what He has honoured her.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[74] ﴿When the fear had left Ibrahim and the good tidings had come to him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lut.﴾

﴿When the fear had left Ibrahim﴾, that is, the apprehension (*khifah*) that they might intend him harm, given that he had recognized them. ﴿And the good tidings had come to him﴾, that is, in place of the fear. ﴿He began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lut﴾, that is, concerning their destruction, seeking to soften Our resolve and to avert it.

It has been related that he said: "Will You destroy the righteous along with the wicked? Will You destroy them when there are fifty righteous among them? Far be it from You!"

It was said to him: "If fifty righteous are found among them, We will pardon all of them for their sake."

He said: "Or forty?"

It was said: "Or forty!"

And so on, until he said: "Or ten." It was said to him: "We will not destroy it for the sake of ten. Yet there are not ten righteous in it; rather, all of them are immersed in indecency." He said: "But Lut is in it!" It was said: "We know best who is in it; We will surely save him."

The phrase ﴿yujadilunā﴾ (he pleads with Us) is the response (*jawab*) of ﴿lammā﴾ (when), and it is stated in the present tense for the sake of *hikayat al-hal* (narrating the present state as it was happening). Alternatively, ﴿lammā﴾ is like ﴿law﴾ (if), which converts the present tense into the past, just as ﴿in﴾ (if) converts the past tense into the future. Or the response is omitted, and what is mentioned here is evidence for it, or is related to it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 11, verse 75:

(p-3468) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[75] ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving, and turning back (to Allah).﴾

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing﴾ i.e., not hasty in seeking retribution against the one who does wrong. ﴿Grieving﴾ (awwah) means one who greatly laments. ﴿Turning back﴾ (munib) means one who returns to Allah in everything He loves and is pleased with. The purpose of enumerating his noble attributes mentioned here is to show what moved him to argue, namely tenderness of heart and excessive compassion.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 11, verse 76:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[76] ﴿O Ibrahim, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will reach them a punishment that cannot be turned back.﴾

﴿O Ibrahim﴾, i.e., it was said to him: O Ibrahim. ﴿Turn away from this﴾, i.e., the disputing. ﴿Indeed, the command of your Lord has come﴾, i.e., His judgment of their destruction. ﴿And indeed, there will reach them a punishment that cannot be turned back﴾, i.e., not by disputing, nor by supplication, nor by anything else.

Benefits:

Some of the exegetes said: These verses have fruits. Among them: the attainment of a child specially favored is a blessing, and the destruction of the disobedient is a blessing, because the glad tidings have been interpreted as the birth of Ishaq, as at the end of the verse, which is: ﴿So We gave him good tidings of Ishaq﴾ [Hud: 71], etc., and they have been interpreted as the destruction of the people of Lut.

Among them: the recommendation of the bringer of good news descending upon the one given the good news, because God sent the angels with that.

Among them: it is recommended for the one given good news to receive it with obedience, in gratitude to God, exalted is He, for what he was given good news of.

Al-Asamm related that they came to him in a land where he was working, and when he finished he stuck his spade (misha, a digging tool) into the ground and prayed two rak'ahs.

Among them: that greeting is legislated, and that the response should be better; due to the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿Peace﴾ [Hud: 69] with the nominative case, as its secret has previously been explained — end of quote.

(p-3469) Among them: the legislation of hospitality, and hastening to it, and the recommendation of the guest hastening to eat from it.

Among them: the recommendation of serving the guest, even if by a woman, due to the saying of Mujahid, ﴿and his wife was standing﴾ [Hud: 71], i.e., in serving the guests of Ibrahim. He said in (al-Wajiz): They did not veil themselves, as was the custom of the Arabs and the practice of the desert dwellers; or she was an elderly woman; and serving guests is among the noble moral qualities.

Among them: the permissibility of a woman conversing with non-related men, and that her voice is not an 'awrah. Thus it is in (al-Iklil).

Among them: that a man's wife is from among his household, so his wives, upon him be prayer and peace, are from among his household. This also comes in the verse ﴿So travel with your family﴾ [Hud: 81].

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 11, verse 77:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them, and said, "This is a trying day."﴾

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot﴾ meaning: after their departure from Abraham, peace be upon him. Lot was residing in the Oak of Mamre (Balluṭ Mamrā), which is in Hebron (Ḥabrūn), the city known today as al-Khalil (the Friend, i.e., Hebron). ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾ meaning: their coming troubled him, because they came to him in the form of beardless youths of handsome faces, and he feared that his people would target them, since he thought they were human beings. ﴿And felt helpless for them﴾ It is said: "ḍāqa bil-amr dharʿuhu wa dhirāʿuhu" and "ḍāqa bihi dharʿan," meaning his capacity weakened, and he found no way out from the disliked matter.

Al-Jawhari said: The original meaning of dhar' is the extending of the hand, as if you mean: you extended your hand toward it but did not reach it. It was also said: the basis of the metaphor is that a person with a short arm cannot reach what a person with a long arm reaches, nor can he bear his strength, so it was used as a proverb for one whose power has fallen short of reaching the matter and being able to deal with it.

Al-Azhari said: dhar' is used in the place of capacity. Its origin is that a camel stretches its forelegs in its stride (p-3470) to a length according to the width of its step; when it is loaded with more than its capacity, it becomes incapable of bearing it and its neck stretches out, so the narrowness of the dhar' became an expression for the narrowness of one's means and capacity.

And ﴿dharʿan﴾ is a specifier (tamyīz), because it came out explaining and transferred (from the subject). The original was: "ḍāqa dharʿī bihi" (my dhar' was narrowed by it). As evidence for the usage of dhirāʿ, the poet said:

Even if he spent a night in a wilderness, it did not narrow his dhirāʿ with it, nor did he rise in the morning humbled by it.

﴿And he said, "This is a trying day."﴾ meaning: difficult. And how could it not be difficult for him, when the dreaded matter had befallen him, as the Exalted said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 11, verse 78:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[78] ﴿And his people came hastening toward him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of reason?"﴾

﴿And his people came hastening toward him﴾ i.e., they hurried, as if they were being driven forward. It is also recited in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il), i.e., yahra'una (ya'rifuna?) as a variant reading. ﴿And before that﴾ i.e., before their coming ﴿they had been doing evil deeds﴾ i.e., grave immoralities, and they were increasing in them (p-3471), so they had become accustomed to them, and their sense of their ugliness had diminished. Therefore they came hastening and openly, with no shame restraining them. Thus the sentence is parenthetical, serving to emphasize what precedes it. It has been said that it explains the reason for his distress, i.e., because Lot knew their habit of committing immoralities before that. ﴿He said﴾ i.e., Lot ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾ He intended to shield his guests with his daughters, and that is the utmost of generosity, i.e., "marry them." Or it was an exaggeration in his humility toward them, and a display of the intensity of his distress at what they had brought upon him, hoping that they would feel shame before him and be moved by pity when they heard this, so that they would leave his guests. This is the summary of what is in al-Kashshaf and those who followed it. It is evident that he, peace be upon him, was confident that his people would not prefer them in any way, however much he praised, extended, urged and encouraged. So his offering of his daughters to shield his guests and ransom them with them, despite his confidence and certainty, was an exaggeration in caring for their protection and a fulfillment of duty in such a grave and disgraceful affair, whose shame and infamy would endure, by defending them to the greatest extent possible, so that he would not be blamed for negligence, and so that it would be known that there is no further recourse for one who has no support from a clan or tribe. That is the ultimate limit in their protection and safeguarding.

In His saying ﴿they are purer for you﴾ there is an element of enticement, in the presence of his guests and within their hearing, and of the increase in generosity and honor and the observance of protection. In sum, it is an encouragement toward what is practically impossible to occur, and an excuse for his guests outwardly, and Allah knows best. In this there is guidance toward purification through the prescribed ways, which is marriage, and an indication of the extreme shamelessness of those people, by which they deserved the seizure that was to come upon them.

﴿So fear Allah﴾ i.e., lest you disobey Him with what is worse in wickedness than fornication.

﴿And do not disgrace me concerning my guests﴾ i.e., do not humiliate and shame me regarding them, for if a man's guest or neighbor is disgraced, the man himself is disgraced, and this is from the nobility of generosity and the genuineness of manliness. ﴿Do not disgrace me﴾ is jussive by the deletion of the nun, and the yā' is deleted, being satisfied with the kasra; it is also recited with the yā' retained, according to the original form.

﴿Is there not among you a man of reason?﴾ i.e., one who would refrain from the ugly and be guided to the right course.

(p-3472) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[79] ﴿They said: "You certainly know that we have no need (lit. no right) regarding your daughters, and you indeed know what we want."﴾

﴿They said: "You certainly know that we have no claim regarding your daughters"﴾ — i.e., no need, since we have no desire for them. In opening their speech with the lam (of emphasis), which signals that what follows is the answer to an oath, i.e., "By Allah, you certainly know," it points to what we have mentioned: that he was confident and certain that they had no desire for them. Their words, ﴿and you indeed know what we want﴾, reinforce this, citing his knowledge as evidence.

The Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[80] ﴿He said: "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a mighty support."﴾

﴿He said: "If only I had power against you"﴾ meaning: power to repel you, by physical strength or by offspring. ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty support﴾ meaning: a large clan, for he was a stranger among his people. He likened it to the base of a mountain in its strength and its protection. That is: I would have done to you what I did, and acted as I acted.

Note:

The Imam Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him, said in (al-Milal):

Some sects thought that what came in the sound hadith, from his ﷺ saying: "May Allah have mercy on Lut, for he used to take refuge in a mighty support," was a rebuke of Lut, peace be upon him. There is no contradiction between the two statements; rather both are true, because Lut, peace be upon him, only sought an immediate protection by which he could hold back his people from the abominations they were engaged in, whether through kinship, clan, or believing followers. Lut, peace be upon him, never ignorantly failed to know that he was taking refuge with his Lord, the Exalted, in the strongest power and the mightiest support. There is no fault on Lut, peace be upon him, in seeking power from people, for Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would be corrupted﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251]. This is what Lut, peace be upon him, sought. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ also sought protection from the Ansar and the Muhajirun so that he might convey the words of his Lord, the Exalted. How, then, is Lut, peace be upon him, rebuked for a matter that he himself did? By Allah! The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not deny this; he only informed that Lut used to take refuge in a mighty support, meaning Allah's help to him through the angels. Lut had not known of that. Whoever believes that Lut thought he had no mighty support from Allah has disbelieved, since this disbelief would be attributed to one of the prophets. This too is a foolish assumption, for it is impossible to suppose that about a Lord who showed him the miracles and whom he constantly called upon. End.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 11, verse 81:**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[81] ﴿They said, "O Lut, indeed we are messengers from your Lord; they will never reach you. So travel with your family during a part of the night, and let not anyone among you look back, except your wife. Indeed, what strikes them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾

﴿They said, "O Lut, indeed we are messengers from your Lord; they will never reach you"﴾ meaning: they will never reach you to harm you, since we are the ones who will harm them. ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night﴾ meaning: during a portion of its latter part, that is, during the remnant of darkness near the dawn (al-saḥar), which is the time when they are deeply immersed in sleep, so they will not be able to confront him or his family. The reading "fa-asri" (فَأسْرِ) has been recited with both qaṭ' (cutting the hamza) and waṣl (connecting it).

﴿And let not anyone among you look back﴾ meaning: let him not look behind him, lest the effect of what descended upon them reach him. ﴿Except your wife; indeed, what strikes them will strike her﴾ meaning: of the punishment. For when she heard the crash of the punishment, she turned around, and so she perished.

Al-Iklil (al-Iklil fi Istinbat al-Tanzil) said: In this is the indication that the wife and the children are included among the family (ahl).

(p-3474) ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning; is not the morning near?﴾ meaning: their appointed time for destruction is the morning. The sentence works as a reason (ta'lil) for the command to travel by night, or as a response to Lut's urgency and his impatience for the punishment, or it was mentioned so that he would hasten in the journey, for the nearness of dawn calls for speed in traveling, in order to distance oneself from the place of the punishment.

On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:
